prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, which opened a route to timekeeping at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks rest on a clean atomic-physics idea: trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so that the lattice light shift cancels on the clock transition, while Doppler and recoil effects are suppressed and thousands of atoms are interrogated at once. Katori made the decisive proposal and early demonstrations, and Ye's group turned it into the benchmark for accuracy, stability and controlled many-body shifts. Fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 have been reproduced in several laboratories, which is the strongest evidence of maturity a measurement discovery can have. The payoff is concrete: tests of fundamental constants and of relativity, centimetre-scale relativistic geodesy, and the basis for a future redefinition of the second. The two-person credit is unusually clean. This is also the one candidate on which the opening ballots converge across subfields: three first places, six top-three rankings, and ranking by all eight members, including those outside atomic physics. I take that as supporting evidence only. My case rests on the physics, and I would argue it even if no colleague had ranked it first.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is overlap with earlier recognition of precision spectroscopy. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb and the 2012 prize covered control of single trapped ions, and a committee could reasonably say that optical clocks are an application of those advances rather than a new discovery. I do not accept that, because the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct concept that neither prize covered, but I take the objection seriously. A second weakness is attribution. Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Hinkley, Ushijima and the ion-clock groups also contributed to the clock's performance, and two names cannot represent them all. A third is that the formal redefinition of the second has not occurred, so some may see the impact as prospective. I treat that as a timing question rather than a flaw in the science.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube (B020) first as an instrument-driven discovery that opened a new observational window, and ranks the lattice clock second while noting possible duplication with the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I agree that the neutrino window is a genuine discovery, and I share his worry about prize overlap, but I read the overlap differently. The comb recognised in 2005 is the ruler, and the 2012 ion work is a different clock architecture. Neither contains the lattice idea, which is what gives the many-atom statistics and 1e-18 stability. I am more troubled by the IceCube credit. Halzen, Karle and Spiering are three arguable choices from a very large collaboration, and Danielsson himself leaves the third place open. Until I see an allocation that the committee finds defensible, I place B020 below the lattice clock, although I would not rule it out.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube first, as the clean discovery of a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos with multi-messenger consequences, and ranks the lattice clock only sixth.
responses.response: I accept that the existence of astrophysical neutrinos is established and that the source associations strengthen the case. But I disagree with ranking the lattice clock as low as sixth if the reason is that it is an application. Making a quantum system whose frequency is known to 18 digits required a new idea about light shifts and a decade of work on many-body and blackbody systematics, and that is physics, not just engineering. If Danielsson's concern is that precision metrology looks incremental, I would ask which part of the clock work is incremental. If it is credit, then the clock has a cleaner two-person allocation than IceCube.

responses.point: Kroll also ranks the lattice clock first, and credits Katori with the magic-wavelength proposal and Ye with record accuracy and many-body clock work, while acknowledging Lemonde and others.
responses.response: We agree on the main points, so I should test the shared view rather than repeat it. I would not name Lemonde in the citation. His group's contributions to lattice-clock accuracy are real, but the committee needs a prize that names the concept and its realization, and the proposal and the leading demonstrations are what the two credited names carry. I would also not lean on the redefinition of the second. It is a consequence still pending, and the case should stand on what has already been measured. I would be glad to hear whether Kroll thinks the credit can survive scrutiny from experts in the metrology community.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the lattice clock first and Car-Parrinello (B022) second, praising the two-author clean credit of Car-Parrinello and its enormous impact, while asking whether a method counts as physics.
responses.response: I share his respect for the Car-Parrinello credit, which is cleaner than almost anything else on the list. My reservation is the discipline question rather than merit. It is a computational method whose main uses are in chemistry and materials science, and I think the committee will have to decide whether it fits a physics prize. That is a judgement about scope and I am not certain of it, so I list B022 only as a point to be debated. I put B004 and B058 as my alternatives because I find them stronger on physical novelty in a combined prize, but I am willing to hear a more detailed argument that a method deserves precedence.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron optics (B025) first as a clear instrument invention that fits the invention route of the prize, and ranks the lattice clock third.
responses.response: I agree that the prize explicitly admits inventions, and that the lattice clock should be judged on the same basis as the corrector. By that standard the clock is also an invention that created a new measurement capability, and arguably one that has led to more new physics, through tests of fundamental constants and time-dilation measurements. My reservation about B025 is the opening support. It was ranked first by only one member and appears elsewhere on none of the eight ballots, so the committee has little cross-subfield evidence for it. I would also like to know how the credit between the TEM and STEM correction lines is to be divided, since the supplied credit seems to leave one of them out.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the 2005 comb and 2012 trapped-ion prizes as having already covered optical clock metrology, which I cannot settle from the supplied text.
Whether other lattice-clock groups, such as Lemonde, Lisdat or the JILA co-authors, should be credited alongside Katori and Ye, and whether the two-name allocation holds under expert scrutiny.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should count as a timing argument for or against awarding the prize now.
I recall the 2005 and 2012 prize citations from memory and have not checked them independently.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile. My documented collaborations are with L'Huillier, the Lund attosecond group, Keller's group at ETH Zurich, Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti and Indelicato, none of whom are credited in B030. I did collaborate in attosecond photoionisation, which is a neighbouring field but not a candidate on this shortlist. I flag my general professional proximity to precision atomic physics and to ETH and Lund experimental groups so the chair can decide whether any recusal is required.
